newsitem.title: GERMANY: Analysts mildly bullish for 1997 aluminium market.
newsitem.headline: Analysts mildly bullish for 1997 aluminium market.

text.p: Aluminium prices in 1997 would move higher amid a recovery in underlying demand and the end of current destocking, two British analysts told Reuters during a Metal Bulletin conference here.
"This year the price will average 77 cents a pound and we're certainly expecting to see prices well above that next year and in 1998," said Adam Rowley of Macquarie Bank Group.
Alan Williamson of Bain & Co, a unit of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said his current 1997 price forecast in cents would be "probably in the mid- to high 80s."
"We could see western world consumption grow by four percent of more next year, based on synchronised economic growth in the main economic regions," Rowley said.
"Also we've had this tremendous destocking phase throughout the supply chain...which is now coming to an end and there is even a possibility of a modest restocking phase."
The analysts also agreed that 1997 prices would take suport from anticipated reductions in Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) exports from unexpected highs this year.

Williamson said the level of Russian exports alone of 1.3 milion tonnes in the first half of 1996 was up 30 percent fom a year earlier and must have been due to a depletion of stockpiles. This process would slow in 1997.
Rowley said his estimate for CIS exports in first half 1997 was 1.2 million tonnes versus 1.4 million in the same 1996 period.

The analysts disagreed with a capacity growth forecast made earlier today by analyst Tony Bird, who pegged growth at 1.5 percent each year over the 1995-2001 period and demand growth at 3.6 percent over the 1990-2006 period.
"That (capacity figure) is possibly an underestimate, you should see greater growth than 1.5 percent a year," said Rowley.
Current prices would not justify widespread closure and there could also be a "capacity creep," where existing smelters raised their output in small quantities, he said.
Modest aluminium market deficits might be shaping up in the next few years, but there would not be a sudden crisis.
Williamson saw a need for some new capacity within a short time span.
"But the expansions we're going to see in the next years should be enough to bring the market close to balance," he believed.
